newsitem.title: USA: Wolfensohn says World Bank facing smaller earnings.
newsitem.headline: Wolfensohn says World Bank facing smaller earnings.

text.p: World Bank President James Wolfensohn on Tuesday said that the lending institution was earning little or no money from its loans because of its pricing structure, and that it was facing a smaller income.

At the same time, Wolfensohn, in a press conference following a joint meeting of the World Bank and International Monetary Fund development committee, said there are additional claims being placed on the institution on a regular basis.
He emphasized that the Bank was on firm footing so far, but he believed it was important to begin the discussion on how some of these issues should be addressed.
"I have absolutely no concerns at all about the financial stability or strength of the bank," he said. "What I have concerns about are constant demands for income."
He said he wanted to draw attention to the bank's executive board that it was not "some miracle institution that continues to produce profits no matter what it does."

Wolfensohn said that he told the board that the way the bank charges for loans is leading to a decline in interest income. "The simple fact is, in the method of pricing for loans, we are very limited, we make no money at it."
The World Bank borrows money in the financial markets and loans the money to countries at small margins for development.
"We used to make money when we charged fixed rates...but today we lend at small margins, so you cannot make a lot of money, you can't make any money."
As an example, he said if the bank's lending was $15 billion, the return at about 1/4 percent is only $37.5 million.
In a statement, the development committee said that improving the climate for private investment was central to developing countries.
It noted that the Bank was preparing a report on improving conditions for private sector investment in infrastructure ahead of the IMF/World Bank annual meeting in Hong Kong in September.
"There is a huge need to attract private investment in infrastructure," Wolfensohn said.
"Before you start talking dollars you've got to get a framework that is friendly," he added.
